QF.id: Taxation of Debt and Equity Products_4

question.text: Amit, a resident individual in the 30% tax bracket, earned the following income in FY 2025-26: (i) Dividend of Rs.8,000 from equity mutual fund, (ii) Dividend of Rs.3,000 from a listed company. What is the TDS deducted on these dividends?

answer.text: Rs.800 on mutual fund dividend; Rs.300 on company dividend — total Rs.1,100
Rs.800 on mutual fund dividend; Nil on company dividend — total Rs.800
Nil on mutual fund dividend; Rs.300 on company dividend — total Rs.300
Nil on both as total dividend is below Rs.15,000

explanation.text: The Logic: Dividend income is taxable in the hands of the recipient, and the payer is required to deduct TDS at 10% under Section 194 (for dividends paid by companies) and Section 194K (for income distributed by mutual funds), subject to a Rs.5,000 per-payer threshold in a financial year for resident individuals. Applying this to Amit: the MF dividend of Rs.8,000 exceeds the Rs.5,000 threshold, so TDS = 10% × Rs.8,000 = Rs.800; the company dividend of Rs.3,000 is below Rs.5,000, so no TDS is deducted on that payment. The total TDS is Rs.800. The Trap: "Rs.800 + Rs.300" wrongly applies TDS to the Rs.3,000 company dividend even though it is below the threshold. "Nil on MF + Rs.300 on company" reverses the threshold application. "Nil on both as total dividend is below Rs.15,000" combines both payers into one threshold and uses an incorrect aggregate figure — the threshold operates per payer, not on a combined basis. Note: The cited NISM Series X-B Investment Adviser Level 2 workbook pages support the principles that dividend income is taxable in the holder's hands and that TDS applies under Sections 194/194K, but the cited pages do not state the Rs.5,000 per-payer TDS threshold with the granularity used in this numerical example. The Rs.5,000 threshold above is referenced from the Income Tax Act provisions as general direct-tax knowledge, not as a workbook-page citation.
